Both landed, working tree clean.

## 1. Roadmap correction — [0b0ab67](architecture/ROADMAP.md)

Tier 0's gating item was still described as "in progress" a week after it shipped. Marked shipped with the measured number (30 min → 78s, `2c37dc6`). I kept the "not customer-viable as is" flag on the heading rather than deleting it, and added a status note explaining why: that flag was a judgement about repos 10–100× this size, not about wall time on your machine, and items 2–4 are still what a large repo would hit. Deleting it would overclaim.

## 2. The annotate form — [07e8911](packages/review-ui/src/components/AnnotateForm.tsx)

It lives on the **change route**, not the maintenance panel — you read a change, see "no reasoning recorded for this change yet", and fix it in place. Collects summary, why, constraints, tested, considered-and-rejected pairs, and the three flags. The endpoint gained `tested` passthrough in the same change; it was missing from the translation layer despite being the field the change page most prominently shows as empty.

Three decisions worth your eye:

- **It says that saving appends.** The form seeds from the current entry and states that saving adds a corrected version while the old one stays readable. A form that looks like it edits, but appends, teaches the wrong model of the data.
- **No author fields.** A form submission is recorded as a human's. Letting a GUI claim an agent wrote something would be a provenance lie with a nice widget — asserted in the test, not just intended.
- **Half-records are refused, not trimmed.** A rejected alternative missing its reason, an option containing the `::` the CLI splits on, a confidence that isn't 0–1 — each stops the save with a sentence naming the fix. Those rules are pure functions in `lib/annotate.ts`, unit-tested there (this package tests logic, not rendering, so I followed that).

**Verified in a real desktop-mode server**, not just in tests: the form renders seeded on the change route with a launch token; a reload without one renders the same page with zero annotate elements; the half-filled-alternative refusal fired in the live page. Refs stayed byte-identical throughout — nothing valid was submitted. 726 tests pass, 4 skipped.

## 3. Your open question, recorded

`ask` as a semi-persistent Q&A surface is now an **OPEN QUESTION in ROADMAP Tier 1**, cross-referenced from ASK_TOOLS §6.1 — recorded, not decided. I wrote down the four things that have to be settled first: where a thread lives (derived data, so `.git-for-ai/`, not a ref), whether an answer is ever worth *promoting* into an annotation rather than auto-captured (the ledger is for why a change was made; filling it with Q&A would blur the one thing that makes it valuable), staleness of cited sources across a long thread, and what a thread even means on three surfaces with three lifetimes — CLI process, browser panel, MCP session, which has no session concept today.

## Next on the desktop track

**Guided repair**: `relink` and `reconcile` are served by the API and still have no UI; they belong on attention items, which is now the last piece before step 5. Packaging after that — but it needs the product-name decision first, since the installer name and app id bake it in.

git commit -F - <<'EOF'
The checkup moves to where the problems are, and offers to fix them

Guided repair, the last of the served-but-unreachable verbs and the end of DESKTOP.md
step 4. `relink` and `reconcile` have had endpoints since the action panel landed; nothing
in the app could reach them. Now a finding that has a repair carries the offer.

The checkup moved OUT of the maintenance panel and INTO the attention inbox, which is
where §3 item 4 always put it ("doctor rendered as the attention inbox's 'run a checkup'
source"). What a checkup finds belongs beside the other things needing a person, and two
buttons for one action in two places is worse than one in the right place. The panel keeps
update-search and fetch/send.

The load-bearing decision is on the CLI side, not the UI's: DoctorCheck gained an optional
`repairs: DoctorRepair[]` — the same advice `remediation` states in prose, as data (the
action, a one-sentence what, whether a commit must be supplied, and the change-ids the
finding is about). Doctor already did the analysis; having the UI re-derive which fix
applies by parsing doctor's English would have been exactly the guessing this project
avoids, and would break the moment a sentence was reworded. A finding with no mechanical
repair carries none and still shows its prose remediation — "here is what is wrong and no
button fixes it" is information.

The flow is deliberately three steps, not one button:

  1. Run a checkup — nothing is inspected until asked.
  2. Read what it found, in plain language, with the changes it names.
  3. Repair, having seen the exact command. These verbs rewrite identity records, so the
     command is rendered before it runs, and is selectable for anyone who would rather do
     it in a terminal.

What is never guessed: which commit is the right one. `relink` asks for it (and for which
change, when doctor named more than one); only `reconcile`, which takes no arguments, is a
single button. After a repair lands the checkup re-runs itself — the fresh finding list is
the evidence, and a stale one beside a "Done." would be a small lie.

Verified end to end against a throwaway repo built with a real unreachable head (squash-
merge-then-delete, the DESKTOP.md G1 class): the checkup found 3 things, exactly one
offered a fix, the preview read `git for-ai relink 68f203b6… HEAD`, running it healed the
change, the checkup re-ran on its own, and the identity finding was gone. The two findings
with no mechanical repair (no Claude settings, index never built) correctly showed prose
and no button. Gated like every write surface: capability flag AND launch token, so
browser mode shows none of it.

718 tests (4 skipped). Docs: DESKTOP.md step 4 complete (steps 1-4 done; only packaging
remains, gated on the product name), REVIEW_UI.md §4.4, ROADMAP desktop entry.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
EOF
